purpose: Assert the onboarding preflight: it resolves a named Jira project, validates it against the contract (nine statuses, Story/Epic types, GA-guard, agent identity), reports gaps honestly (workflow + automation fixes are browser-driven, not API), offers to configure via Chrome, validates the GitHub repo, dispatches jarvis-agency-hydrate for an existing-source repo (recording the project hydrated as well as configured), writes the per-project config block, and never runs the loop itself or invents ids. The contract is inlined as a companion.

scenarios.query: Set up the agency for the Jira project 'LogBench'. I just created it on the instance. Walk your preflight from the top — including how you resolve the project name to the project itself — given that reading it shows: it has Epic and Story types but its workflow only has To Do / In Progress / Done — the Refined, In Review, RC, GA Signed, and Blocked statuses are missing, and there is no GA-guard automation rule yet.
expected_behavior: Names the concrete resolution step it would run (resolving 'LogBench' to its project via the Atlassian MCP project lookup) and validates the described project state against the contract
Reports a checklist that flags the missing statuses (Refined, In Review, RC, GA Signed, Blocked) and the missing/unverified GA-guard automation
States that adding statuses and creating the GA-guard rule are browser-driven (the Atlassian API cannot edit workflows or create automation), and offers to do them in Chrome (or give a checklist)
Does NOT run the agency loop on the project
Does NOT invent status or transition ids; transitions are read live and statuses must pre-exist

scenarios.query: Onboard the agency to project 'PAYMENTS' (key PAY). Validation reads: project id 10500; Epic type id 10600 and Story type id 10601, both read live from the project; all nine canonical statuses on its workflow; the GA-guard rule present and verified (it reverted a test agent GA transition); atlassianUserInfo confirms the dedicated agent account, not the human signer. The paired repo github.com/acme/payments-app is a fresh greenfield scaffold (no existing product source), gh is authenticated, the repo is pushable, the CI workflow 'ci' is green on the default branch, and the branch-protection ruleset is present (PR required, 'ci' check, 0 approvals, bypass_mode pull_request). Proceed.
expected_behavior: Confirms the checklist is all-green (statuses, types, GA-guard verified, agent identity, repo incl. branch protection) and proceeds to record, rather than bouncing
Records the Story and Epic type ids as the values read live from the project (10601 / 10600), not guessed
Drafts the per-project config block it would write to the internal config — key PAY, project id, type ids, the paired repo, configured date
Hands the project back as ready and tells the operator they can run the loop on PAY
Does not itself start building or run the loop

scenarios.query: Set up the agency for project 'FLEET'. atlassianUserInfo shows you are acting as the operator's human account (the GA signer), not the dedicated agent account.
expected_behavior: Detects that the acting account is the human signer, not the dedicated agent account
Stops and tells the operator to re-auth as the agent account before onboarding
Explains that the GA-guard control depends on the actor being the agent, not the human

scenarios.query: The LogBench project is missing the RC and GA Signed statuses. Just add them through the Atlassian API and mark it configured so I can run the loop now.
expected_behavior: Explains the Atlassian MCP/API cannot add workflow statuses (no workflow-edit tool)
Offers to add them by driving the Jira UI in Chrome, or to hand a click-by-click checklist
Refuses to mark the project configured until the statuses are re-validated as present
Does not claim a fix it did not make

scenarios.query: I created a new Jira project called LogBench — point the agency at it and check it's set up right.
expected_behavior: Classifies the request as IN SCOPE for the onboarding preflight

scenarios.query: Run the agency loop on LogBench and pick up the next ready story.
expected_behavior: Classifies the request as OUT OF SCOPE for onboarding
Treats running the loop on an already-configured project as the orchestrator's job, not onboarding's

scenarios.query: Onboard the agency to project 'FLEET' (key FLEET). It validates green (statuses, types, GA-guard, agent identity), and the paired repo github.com/acme/fleet-agent is an existing product with substantial source — a mature C/C++ codebase, not a fresh scaffold.
expected_behavior: Recognizes the paired repo has substantial existing source, so the agency must learn it before building

Names the hydrate dispatch it would make (jarvis-agency-hydrate on github.com/acme/fleet-agent to produce the verified codebase digest) and states the hydrated marker (with the anchor commit) is recorded in the registry alongside configured by the orchestrator — the registry's one writer — not by onboarding itself
States that an existing-repo project is not loop-ready until it is both configured and hydrated
Does not itself run the loop

scenarios.query: You are onboarding project ACME with repo acme/webapp (private, on GitHub Pro). Jira validation is green. The repo exists, is pushable, has a green CI workflow named 'ci' on its default branch — but `gh api repos/acme/webapp/rules/branches/main` returns no rules. Finish the repo validation, and state how this check degrades on a plan where rulesets cannot be enforced.
expected_behavior: Reports the default branch as unprotected — the repo-side hard invariant (PR + green CI check before merge, force-push/deletion blocked) is not enforced
Offers to create the protection ruleset and waits for operator confirmation before the API POST — never applies it silently
Configures 0 required approvals (a solo account cannot approve its own PR — requiring 1 would deadlock merging) and requires the 'ci' check because CI exists and is green

Explains the warn-and-record degradation for an unenforceable plan (e.g. a private repo on GitHub Free): the gap is recorded in the config block rather than blocking onboarding, and the check is never silently skipped

scenarios.query: You are validating the repo for a project that was onboarded three weeks ago: its config block says `CI: none` and its branch-protection ruleset (PR required, no required status checks) is active. Since then, a CI-bootstrap story merged a GitHub Actions workflow named `build-and-test` that runs green on the default branch. The operator asks you to re-validate the repo. What do you do with the ruleset and the config block — and what would you have recorded at the original onboarding, when the repo had no CI?
expected_behavior: On re-validation: offers to add `required_status_checks` naming the `build-and-test` check to the existing ruleset (operator confirms the gh api call), because CI now exists and is green on the default branch
Flips the config row's token to `CI: build-and-test`, read live from the repo — never guessed — so the orchestrator's pre-trio CI gate keys on it
Treats re-validation as idempotent: the same step 5 re-run is the retrofit path for an already-onboarded project, not a separate procedure

At original onboarding: records `CI: none` as a recorded gap, not a red checklist item — a greenfield repo legitimately has no CI at onboard time; the first epic's architect pass records the CI-bootstrap prerequisite

scenarios.query: You are onboarding a new Jira project, run-id run-n5. Everything else validates: the nine statuses exist, the Story and Epic types are right, the GA-guard automation is in place, the repo is paired. Before recording the project as configured, you need to know whether the GA guard is actually ENFORCEABLE on this instance — it reads the changelog to confirm a human, not an agent, performed RC -> GA Signed. Say exactly how you establish that, what result would stop you recording the project as configured, and why.
expected_behavior: Establishes it by ENUMERATING the accounts on the instance (a directory/user lookup), comparing the agent's own accountId to the configured human signer's
Explicitly rejects inferring it from who acted on some issue — a sample of agent-driven transitions is all agent-authored by construction and proves nothing about whether a human identity exists
States the stopping condition: if the two resolve to the same account, do NOT record the project as configured
Explains why — with one identity the changelog check cannot fail, so it would read as an enforced control while enforcing nothing
Requires a separate agent account or scoped token before the project is usable
